idiom_name: objects with update(dt) walked in a requestAnimationFrame callback
implementation_notes: JavaScript needs no base class: the hook is any update method, the collection is an array, and the driver is a for...of inside the browser's frame callback - requestAnimationFrame 'requests the browser to call a user-supplied callback function before the next repaint' and passes a DOMHighResTimeStamp marking the end of the previous frame's rendering. What replaces the classic structure: duck typing replaces the abstract update hook and the array walk replaces the entity manager, while rAF supplies the frame (the Game Loop concern) and is one-shot, so the callback must re-request itself. A class hierarchy is only worth it when entities share real implementation (a pooled base with position and velocity), which is the part engine libraries such as Phaser package.
pitfalls: rAF is paused in background tabs and hidden iframes, so wall-clock expectations (cooldowns, TTLs) drift from simulation time - accumulate dt rather than reading Date.now().
The timestamp marks the end of the previous frame and is shared by every callback in that frame; subtracting a locally captured performance.now() instead mixes time bases.
splice() during the walk shifts indices and skips the next entity, and pushes can act in the frame that created them: mark dead, then compact after the loop.
setInterval/setTimeout are not synchronised with painting, keep running in the background and can queue up missed ticks - they are not a substitute for rAF.
